states.name: Connecticut
states.note: CUTPA is a broad little-FTC act with fee-shifting and punitive damages; customary foreclosure is judicial.

states.name: Massachusetts
states.note: Chapter 93A plus AG rules that treat unconscionable terms as unfair; double or treble damages for willful or bad-faith violations; 30-day demand letter required; foreclosure is nonjudicial.

states.name: New Jersey
states.note: Consumer Fraud Act mandates treble damages and fees; New Jersey also has the Home Ownership Security Act and judicial foreclosure.

states.name: New Mexico
states.note: Unfair Practices Act is broad and privately enforceable; Home Loan Protection Act adds high-cost mortgage rules.

states.name: Hawaii
states.note: NCLC's only all-strong UDAP statute: unfair and deceptive catch-alls, automatic treble or $1,000, fees, and lender coverage.

states.name: North Dakota
states.note: Consumer fraud law is relatively strong on private remedies; foreclosure is judicial.

states.name: Illinois
states.statute: Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act
states.note: ICFA is a broad, privately enforceable unfair-and-deceptive statute; Illinois also has a High Risk Home Loan Act and judicial foreclosure.

states.name: Vermont
states.note: Broad unfair-and-deceptive Consumer Protection Act with exemplary damages and judicial foreclosure.

states.name: Missouri
states.note: Merchandising Practices Act is a broad, privately enforceable unfair-and-deceptive statute with strong NCLC feature ratings.

states.name: California
states.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200; Cal. Civ. Code § 1750 et seq.
states.note: UCL covers unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent practices; CLRA adds remedies; strong unconscionability doctrine; UCL itself is restitution-only.

states.name: South Carolina
states.note: UTPA plus a high-cost home-loan act and judicial foreclosure; willful violations can be trebled, and a public-interest showing can be required.

states.name: District of Columbia
states.note: CPPA is aggressive (treble damages or $1,500 per violation, plus punitive damages); foreclosure is typically nonjudicial.

states.name: North Carolina
states.statute: Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act
states.note: Automatic treble damages under ch. 75 and the nation's first comprehensive high-cost home-loan statute; reliance can still be a hurdle.

states.name: Washington
states.note: CPA is a broad little-FTC act with fees and limited treble damages (capped at $25,000 for unfair/deceptive violations); a private plaintiff must show a public-interest impact.

states.name: Montana
states.statute: Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Act
states.note: Broad private UDAP remedies, including up to treble damages, with an insurance-coverage gap.

states.name: Idaho
states.note: Broad private UDAP remedies, including fees and punitive damages, with some coverage questions around credit and insurance.

states.name: Michigan
states.note: 2026 Michigan Supreme Court decision restored MCPA coverage of licensed and regulated businesses; still no general treble damages.

states.name: Kansas
states.note: Strong private remedies, including a civil-penalty option; many listed violations still require knowledge or willfulness.

states.name: Maryland
states.cite: Md. Code, Com. Law § 13-101 et seq.
states.apl: Md. Code, Com. Law Title 12 high-cost provisions
states.note: MCPA is privately enforceable, with later expansions; foreclosure is nonjudicial but includes mediation and court ratification.

states.name: Iowa
states.statute: Consumer Fraud Act; ch. 714H private right
states.note: A 2009 private right of action exists (ch. 714H), but it does not reach most lenders, insurers, utilities, or real-estate licensees.

states.name: Arizona
states.note: Broad unfair and deceptive prohibitions and few industry exemptions, but no fee-shifting or multiple damages for private plaintiffs.

states.name: Maine
states.note: Broad UTPA with strong public-enforcement tools; private multiple damages and some fee questions are weaker.

states.name: Ohio
states.note: CSPA offers treble damages, but most lenders and creditors are exempt from the statute.

states.name: Pennsylvania
states.note: UTPCPL catch-all plus treble damages and fees; Gregg (2021) makes deceptive conduct strict liability, but reliance and a strict parol-evidence rule (Yocca) still constrain claims.

states.name: Louisiana
states.note: LUTPA has unfair/deceptive coverage, but banks, insurers, and utilities are largely exempt; treble damages require AG notice.

states.name: Georgia
states.note: Fair Business Practices Act plus the Fair Lending Act; reliance and pre-suit notice are hurdles; foreclosure is nonjudicial.

states.name: Arkansas
states.note: Covers deceptive and unconscionable acts, but 2017 amendments require reliance and actual financial loss and generally bar class actions.

states.name: New Hampshire
states.note: Little-FTC act with multiple damages for willful violations, but lenders, insurers, and utilities are largely exempt.

states.name: Kentucky
states.note: Consumer Protection Act is relatively broad, but consumers cannot enforce it against some industries, including certain lenders.

states.name: Alaska
states.statute: Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Act
states.note: Strong prohibitions and automatic treble damages, offset by a loser-pays fee risk, an insurer exemption, and no coverage of real-estate deals.

states.name: New York
states.note: GBL § 349 is a workhorse deception statute, but consumers do not get a broad unfairness catch-all, treble damages are capped at $1,000, and fee-shifting is limited.

states.name: Oklahoma
states.note: Consumer Protection Act is solid on remedies, with insurance and utility gaps; foreclosure may proceed judicially or by power of sale.

states.name: Rhode Island
states.note: A 2021 amendment strengthened AG tools and damages, but private suits remain barred where the conduct is subject to other agency regulation.

states.name: Utah
states.note: Consumer Sales Practices Act covers unfair and deceptive acts, with insurance and utility gaps and no multiple damages.

states.name: Delaware
states.note: Consumer Fraud Act covers deception broadly, but NCLC found no general unfairness prohibition consumers can use.

states.name: Indiana
states.note: Consumers cannot enforce some key prohibitions; intent and reliance hurdles shrink the Deceptive Consumer Sales Act in practice.

states.name: West Virginia
states.statute: Consumer Credit and Protection Act, Art. 6
states.note: Consumer Credit and Protection Act reaches unfair and deceptive practices, with some coverage ambiguities.

states.name: Nevada
states.note: Deceptive-practices statute lacks a broad unfairness catch-all; AG enforcement can require knowledge or intent.

states.name: Wyoming
states.note: Knowledge is required, individual plaintiffs do not recover attorney fees, and a pre-suit notice applies; AG suits also require knowledge or intent.

states.name: Alabama
states.note: Broad unfair/deceptive ban, but banks and lenders are exempt; pre-suit notice and no class actions; nonjudicial foreclosure.

states.name: Oregon
states.note: No broad privately enforceable unfairness ban, and deception coverage is limited; some industries are hard for consumers to reach.

states.name: Texas
states.cite: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.41 et seq.
states.note: DTPA remedies can be strong, but consumers cannot enforce a general unfairness ban, and some claims require reliance.

states.name: Wisconsin
states.note: Patchwork statutes: consumers can enforce unfairness only via specific state rules, and the economic-loss doctrine applies even to consumers.

states.name: Nebraska
states.note: Most lenders and utilities are exempt; damage enhancements are capped at $1,000 for some claims.

states.name: Colorado
states.note: Laundry-list statute with no general unfairness or deception catch-all; bad-faith trebling exists, but the substantive net is narrow.

states.name: Minnesota
states.note: No general unfairness prohibition; consumer-fraud statute is narrower and often requires a public-interest showing in private suits.

states.name: Florida
states.note: FDUTPA is broad on paper, but lenders and other industries are carved out and losing plaintiffs can owe the business's fees.

states.name: Tennessee
states.note: Consumers cannot enforce the statute's broad prohibitions; listed practices and industry gaps leave a thin private right.

states.name: South Dakota
states.statute: Deceptive Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law
states.note: No unfairness catch-all; deception often requires knowledge or intent; no attorney-fee recovery for individual consumer suits.

states.name: Virginia
states.note: No general unfairness prohibition, and most lenders, insurers, and utilities are exempt; willful violations can be trebled.

states.name: Mississippi
states.note: Among the weakest private remedies: consumers cannot enforce the broad prohibitions, and fees and multiple damages are lacking.
